claim: Wnt7A is the most abundant Wnt in motoneurons
source: Noticeably, Wnt7A appeared to be the most abundant, followed by Wnt3, Wnt4, and Wnt7B.
evidence: Based on real-time PCR analysis of FACS-isolated motoneurons from P0 HB9-tdTomato mice, shown in Figure 1A

claim: Wnt5A and Wnt9A are the dominant Wnts in Schwann cells
source: Dominant Wnts in Schwann cells appeared to be Wnt5A and Wnt9A whereas Wnt4, Wnt6 and Wnt9A were the most abundant in muscle cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Based on real-time PCR analysis of primary Schwann cells from P3 mice, shown in Figure 1B

claim: Wnt4, Wnt6 and Wnt9A are the most abundant Wnts in muscle cells
source: Dominant Wnts in Schwann cells appeared to be Wnt5A and Wnt9A whereas Wnt4, Wnt6 and Wnt9A were the most abundant in muscle cells (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Based on real-time PCR analysis of C2C12 myotubes, shown in Figure 1C

claim: HSA-Wls-/- mice have no apparent NMJ deficits at birth
source: HSA-Wls-/- mice appeared to be normal at birth without apparent deficits in AChR clusters (number and location), motor nerve terminals (arborization) and innervation of AChR clusters (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: Based on whole-mount staining of muscles from P0 mice showing normal NMJ morphology

claim: Muscle Wls is dispensable for NMJ formation
source: These results were in agreement with a previous report (Remédio et al., 2016) and indicate that muscle Wls is dispensable for NMJ formation.
evidence: Based on normal NMJ morphology in HSA-Wls-/- mice and agreement with published literature

claim: Wnt1-Wls-/- mice die soon after birth with craniofacial skeleton defects
source: Wnt1-Wls-/- mice died soon after birth with craniofacial skeleton defects, in accord with the notion that Wnt signaling in neural crests is critical for craniofacial skeleton development (Fu et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on observed phenotype and cited literature on Wnt signaling in neural crests

claim: Wls in Schwann cells is not necessary for NMJ formation
source: However, NMJs in Wnt1-Wls-/- mice were similar to those of control mice in terms of number, location, innervation of AChR clusters and motor nerve arborization (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H). These results suggest that Wls in Schwann cells is not necessary for NMJ formation.
evidence: Based on normal NMJ morphology in Wnt1-Wls-/- mice shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G and H

claim: Wls protein is reduced in sciatic nerves of HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Western blotting of sciatic nerve homogenates revealed a reduction of Wls protein (Figure 2B).
evidence: Based on Western blot analysis shown in Figure 2B

claim: Wls is ablated from motoneurons in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: As shown in Figure 2C, Wls was readily detectable in ChAT positive motoneurons in ventral horns of the spinal cord of control mice, but not those of HB9-Wls-/- mice. These results indicate that Wls was ablated from motoneurons in HB9-Wls-/- mice.
evidence: Based on immunostaining of spinal cord sections showing loss of Wls in ChAT-positive motoneurons

claim: HB9-Wls-/- pups show growth retardation with smaller body sizes as they develop
source: However, as mice developed, HB9-Wls-/- pups showed growth retardation with smaller body sizes (100.0 ± 2.2% in control vs 68.6 ± 9.4% in HB9-Wls-/-, p<0.01, Figure 2D and E).
evidence: Based on body weight measurements at P7 showing significant reduction in mutant mice

claim: One third of HB9-Wls-/- mice die prematurely before adulthood
source: One third of HB9-Wls-/- mice died prematurely before adulthood.
evidence: Based on survival observations of the mutant mice

claim: Grip strength is reduced by 69% in 2-month-old HB9-Wls-/- mice compared to control
source: In particular, grip strength was reduced by 69%, compared with control (113.4 ± 5.8 g in control mice to 35.2 ± 7.9 g in HB9-Wls-/- mice; p<0.01) (Figure 2F).
evidence: Based on grip strength measurements shown in Figure 2F

claim: HB9-Wls-/- mice have reduced grip strength even when body weights are similar to control
source: As shown in Figure 2G, HB9-Wls-/- mice had reduced grip strength (129 ± 9.7 g in control mice; 71.8 ± 7.9 g in HB9-Wls-/- mice, p<0.01).
evidence: Based on grip strength measurements in mice with similar body weights shown in Figure 2G

claim: Motoneuron Wls is required for development of body weight and muscle strength
source: These results indicate that motoneuron Wls is required for development of body weight and muscle strength.
evidence: Based on reduced body weight and grip strength in HB9-Wls-/- mice

claim: Nerve terminal pathfinding to the middle region of muscle fibers appears grossly normal in E18.5 HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: These results indicate that nerve terminal pathfinding to the middle region of muscle fibers and defasciculation or arborization appears grossly normal.
evidence: Based on morphological analysis of E18.5 diaphragms showing normal nerve terminal localization

claim: The width of the central region occupied by AChR clusters is similar in control and HB9-Wls-/- diaphragms at E18.5
source: The width of the central region that occupied by AChR clusters was similar in control and in HB9-Wls-/- diaphragms (172 ± 25.4 µm vs 198 ± 25.5 µm, p>0.05).
evidence: Based on quantitative measurements of endplate band width at E18.5

claim: The density and size of AChR clusters in HB9-Wls-/- mice are similar to control at E18.5
source: The density and size of AChR clusters in HB9-Wls-/- mice were also similar to those in control mice (AChR size: 100 ± 5.0% vs 87.9 ± 4.3%, p>0.05; AChR density: 537 ± 28.0 vs 556 ± 22.2 per µm2, p>0.05) (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–2D).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of AChR clusters at E18.5 shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2

claim: HB9-Wls-/- mice are able to form NMJs in the absence of motoneuron Wls
source: These results suggest that HB9-Wls-/- mice were able to form the NMJ in the absence of motoneuron Wls, in agreement with the finding of normal body weights of P0 HB9-Wls-/- mice.
evidence: Based on normal NMJ morphology at E18.5 and normal body weight at P0

claim: AChR cluster arrays in 2-month-old HB9-Wls-/- mice are less continuous than control
source: The arrays of HB9-Wls-/- mice appeared to be as complex as control mice, but less continuous (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Based on whole-mount staining of gastrocnemius from 2-month-old mice shown in Figure 3A and B

claim: The number of AChR cluster fragments is increased in 2-month-old HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: There were small pieces of AChR clusters (arrow, Figure 3A and B), and the number of AChR cluster fragments were increased to 3.0 ± 0.3 fragments per NMJ in HB9-Wls-/- mice from 1.4 ± 0.2 fragments per NMJ in control mice (p<0.01) (Figure 3A–3C).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of AChR fragmentation shown in Figure 3C

claim: Abnormal swellings of nerve terminals appear in 53.5% of NMJs in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Unlike axonal shedding which was observed in a small number of NMJs, axonal swellings in HB9-Wls-/- mice were observed in 53.5 ± 3.2% of nerve terminals (Figure 3E).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of nerve terminal swellings shown in Figure 3E

claim: Nerve terminals in HB9-Wls-/- mice become detached from AChR arrays
source: In addition to axonal swellings, nerve terminals in HB9-Wls-/- mice became detached from AChR arrays, causing misalignment between nerve terminals and AChR clusters (blue arrowhead, Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on immunostaining showing detachment of nerve terminals from AChR clusters in Figure 3B

claim: The area of AChR arrays covered by nerve terminals is reduced in 2-month-old HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Consequently, the area of AChR arrays that were covered by nerve terminals was reduced in HB9-Wls-/- mice (Figure 3D) (73.6 ± 7.1% in HB9-Wls-/- vs 100 ± 3.7% in control, p<0.05).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of pre/postsynaptic overlap shown in Figure 3D

claim: Synapse elimination is normal in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: We did not find the excessive NMJ number in each single muscle fiber at different ages of HB9-Wls-/- mice, suggesting the normal synapse elimination in HB9-Wls-/- mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of NMJ number per muscle fiber at different ages shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: The number of synaptic vesicles is reduced in nerve terminals of HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Noticeably, the number of synaptic vesicles was reduced in nerve terminals (107 ± 14.6 per µm2 in control vs 25.6 ± 3.0 in HB9-Wls-/-, p<0.01, black arrowhead) (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy analysis of P15 diaphragm NMJs shown in Figure 4

claim: The number of junctional folds is reduced in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: The number of junctional folds was reduced (1.2 ± 0.3 in HB9-Wls-/- vs 3.0 ± 0.5 in control per µm, p<0.05, black arrow) (Figure 4).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: Synaptic cleft width is increased in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Synaptic cleft was uneven in HB9-Wls-/- mice and appeared to be larger than that of control mice (2.1 ± 0.3 folds in HB9-Wls-/- mice, compared with that in control mice, p<0.01) (Figure 4A and D).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 4D

claim: Basal lamina density is reduced without a high-density midline in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: However, in HB9-Wls-/- mice, basal lamina density was reduced without a high-density midline (empty arrowheads, Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on electron microscopy observations shown in Figure 4A

claim: Wls in motoneurons is critical for the integrity of NMJ structure
source: These EM data are in accord with those from light microscopic studies (Figure 3) and demonstrate that Wls in motoneurons is critical for the integrity of NMJ structure.
evidence: Based on multiple structural deficits observed by EM and light microscopy

claim: CMAPs show little change in control mice after 10 consecutive nerve stimuli at frequencies from 2 Hz to 40 Hz
source: In control mice, CMAPs showed little change after 10 consecutive nerve stimuli at frequencies from 2 Hz to 40 Hz (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5A and B

claim: CMAPs in HB9-Wls-/- mice decrease significantly at 40 Hz stimulation
source: While in HB9-Wls-/- mice, CMAPs recorded at 40 Hz began to decrease at the second stimulus and significantly decreased from the fourth; the decrement of CMAP at the tenth stimulus was about 10% (Figure 5B).
evidence: Based on electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 5B

claim: The reduction of CMAPs in HB9-Wls-/- mice is frequency-dependent
source: The reduction of CMAPs in HB9-Wls-/- mice was frequency-dependent (Figure 5C), which indicates progressive loss of successful neuromuscular transmission after repeated stimulation.
evidence: Based on CMAP measurements at different stimulation frequencies shown in Figure 5C

claim: mEPP amplitudes are reduced in P30 HB9-Wls-/- mice compared to control
source: As shown in Figure 5D and E, mEPP amplitudes were reduced in HB9-Wls-/- mice, compared with controls (1.20 ± 0.08 mV in control vs 0.76 ± 0.06 mV in HB9-Wls-/-; p<0.01), indicative of reduced AChR density.
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings from P30 hemidiaphragms shown in Figure 5D and E

claim: mEPP frequencies are decreased by ~40% in P30 HB9-Wls-/- diaphragms compared to control
source: mEPP frequencies were also decreased by ~40% in HB9-Wls-/- diaphragms, compared with control (0.78 ± 0.03 Hz in HB9-Wls-/- vs 1.20 ± 0.08 Hz in control, p<0.01, Figure 5D and F).
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings from P30 hemidiaphragms shown in Figure 5D and F

claim: Reduced mEPP frequency demonstrates deficits in spontaneous ACh release from motor nerve terminals
source: This result demonstrates deficits in spontaneous ACh release from motor nerve terminals, consistent with morphological presynaptic defects in mice lacking Wls in motoneurons.
evidence: Based on reduced mEPP frequency and correlation with morphological findings

claim: mEPP frequency in P1 HB9-Wls-/- NMJs is reduced by 42% compared to control
source: mEPP frequency in HB9-Wls-/- NMJs was reduced by 42% (0.042 ± 0.003 Hz in control vs 0.022 ± 0.002 Hz in mutant, p<0.01) (Figure 5G and I), indicative of presynaptic deficits.
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings from P1 diaphragms shown in Figure 5G and I

claim: There is no significant difference in mEPP amplitudes between control and HB9-Wls-/- mice at P1
source: In contrast, there was no significant difference in mEPP amplitudes between control and HB9-Wls-/- mice (1.98 ± 0.10 mV in control vs 1.88 ± 0.09 mV in HB9-Wls-/-, p>0.05) (Figure 5G and H).
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings from P1 diaphragms shown in Figure 5G and H

claim: Presynaptic deficits occur in advance of postsynaptic deficits in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: These functional results demonstrate that presynaptic deficits occurred in advance of postsynaptic deficits, agreeing the notion that EM and electrophysiological analysis are more sensitive in revealing NMJ deficits than light microscope analysis.
evidence: Based on reduced mEPP frequency but normal amplitude at P1, compared to both being reduced at P30

claim: CCh increases both mEPP frequency and amplitude at P1 and P30 mice
source: CCh (10 µM) increased both mEPP frequency and amplitude at P1 and P30 mice (Figure 5D–5I), in agreement with previous reports (Katz and Miledi, 1972; Miyamoto and Volle, 1974).
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings with CCh treatment shown in Figure 5 and cited literature

claim: CCh elevates mEPP frequency and amplitude in Wls mutant diaphragms to similar or higher levels of controls in the absence of CCh
source: Interestingly, CCh also elevated mEPP frequency and amplitude in Wls mutant diaphragms to similar or higher levels of controls in the absence of CCh (Figure 5D–5I).
evidence: Based on mEPP recordings with CCh treatment shown in Figure 5D-5I

claim: Transmission impairment in mutant mice can be attenuated by ACh agonist
source: These results indicate that transmission impairment in mutant mice could be attenuated by ACh agonist.
evidence: Based on CCh rescue of mEPP deficits in mutant mice

claim: Axonal swellings in HB9-Wls-/- mice are positive for neurofilament
source: As shown in Figure 6A, the swellings were positive for NF, indicating that they may contain neurofilaments.
evidence: Based on immunostaining with anti-NF antibody shown in Figure 6A

claim: Axonal swellings in HB9-Wls-/- mice are covered by Schwann cells
source: They could also be stained with antibody against S100, a marker of Schwann cells, suggesting that the swellings were covered by Schwann cells (Figure 6A).
evidence: Based on immunostaining with anti-S100 antibody shown in Figure 6A

claim: SV2-positive aggregates are present in motoneuron axons of HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Noticeably, SV2-positive aggregates were seen in motoneuron axons in HB9-Wls-/- mice (white arrow, Figure 6B). Such SV2 aggregates were not observed in control mice.
evidence: Based on immunostaining with anti-SV2 antibody shown in Figure 6B

claim: SV2 and Synapsin 1 protein levels in phrenic nerve are increased in HB9-Wls-/- mutant mice compared to control
source: As shown in Figure 6C, compared with control, SV2 and Synapsin 1 protein level in phrenic nerve was increased in HB9-Wls-/- mutant mice.
evidence: Based on Western blot analysis of phrenic nerve shown in Figure 6C

claim: Abnormal accumulation of synaptic vesicles occurs in axons of HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: These results suggest abnormal accumulation of synaptic vesicles in axons.
evidence: Based on increased SV2 and Synapsin 1 levels in axons and SV2-positive aggregates

claim: Wls knockdown reduces Wnt5A, Wnt7A, Wnt7B, Wnt9A, and Wnt9B levels in the medium
source: As shown in Figure 7A and B, Wls knockdown reduced most of Wnts level including Wnt5A, Wnt7A, Wnt7B, Wnt9A, and Wnt9B in the medium, in agreement with previous reports.
evidence: Based on Western blot analysis of conditioned medium from HEK293 cells co-transfected with Wls-shRNA and Wnt constructs shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: Wnt7A and Wnt7B reduce the number of axon swellings in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: Remarkably, muscles injected with Wnt7A and Wnt7B displayed fewer axon swellings, compared with muscles injected with vehicle (Figure 7C and D).
evidence: Based on immunostaining of TA muscles injected with Wnt recombinant proteins shown in Figure 7C and D

claim: Wnt5A and Wnt9B do not reduce axon swellings in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: This effect appeared to be specific because muscles injected Wnt5A or Wnt9B displayed similar number of axon swellings (NMJs with swellings: 22.7 ± 3.0% in HB9-Wls-/-; 17.9 ± 3.9% in HB9-Wls-/- + Wnt5A; 10.1 ± 2.7% in HB9-Wls-/- + Wnt7A; 12.2 ± 1.5 in HB9-Wls-/- + Wnt7B; 19.4 ± 2.4% in HB9-Wls-/- + Wnt9B).
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of axon swellings after Wnt protein injection

claim: CMAPs of HB9-Wls-/- mice are rescued by Wnt7A administration
source: As shown in Figure 7E, CMAPs of HB9-Wls-/- mice were resuced by Wnt7A administration.
evidence: Based on CMAP recordings after Wnt7A injection shown in Figure 7E

claim: Motoneurons release Wnts to regulate NMJ development
source: Together, these results support a model where motoneurons release Wnts to regulate NMJ development.
evidence: Based on NMJ deficits in motoneuron-specific Wls knockout and rescue by Wnt7A/7B

claim: Blocking Wnt secretion from motoneurons causes NMJ degeneration
source: Here we found that blocking Wnt secretion from motoneurons causes NMJ degeneration evidenced by muscle weakness, impaired neurotransmission, distorted NMJ structure, motor axonal terminal swelling, and synaptic vesicle reduction.
evidence: Based on multiple phenotypes observed in HB9-Wls-/- mice

claim: Wnt7A and Wnt7B are key Wnts secreted from motoneurons for NMJ development
source: Rescue experiments identified Wnt7A and Wnt7B as key Wnts secreted from motoneurons for NMJ development.
evidence: Based on rescue of NMJ deficits by Wnt7A and Wnt7B but not other Wnts

claim: Motoneuron Wnts have a novel role in NMJ development and maintenance
source: Our results provide a novel role of Wnt ligand secretion from motoneurons in NMJ development and maintenance.
evidence: Based on the comprehensive findings of the study showing age-dependent NMJ deficits in motoneuron-specific Wls knockout

claim: Motoneuron Wnts cannot be compensated by Wnts from skeletal muscle fibers or Schwann cells
source: These results could suggest that motoneuron Wnts cannot be compensated by Wnts from skeletal muscle fibers or Schwann cells.
evidence: Based on NMJ deficits in motoneuron-specific Wls knockout but not in muscle or Schwann cell-specific knockouts

claim: Wnt7A mainly acts on nerve terminals in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: However, we did not observe a change in AChR cluster size or intensity after Wnt7A injection (data not shown). Rather, Wnt7A reduced the number of axonal swellings and functionally rescued neurotransmission impairment in the HB9-Wls-/-, suggesting that Wnt7A mainly acts on nerve terminals in the mutant.
evidence: Based on rescue of presynaptic but not postsynaptic deficits by Wnt7A injection

claim: The unique presynaptic phenotypes of HB9-Wls-/- mice were not observed in MuSK or Rapsyn mutant mice
source: First, the unique presynaptic phenotypes of HB9-Wls-/- mice - swollen axon terminals and enlarged varicosities were not observed in MuSK or Rapsyn mutant mice where AChR clusters were abolished and nerve terminals arborize extensively (without swellings, however) (DeChiara et al., 1996; Gautam et al., 1995; Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on comparison with published phenotypes of MuSK and Rapsyn mutants

claim: The presynaptic phenotypes of HB9-Wls-/- mice were not observed in muscle-specific β-catenin knockout or transgenic mice
source: Second, they were not observed in muscle-specific β-catenin knockout or transgenic mice overexpressing β-catenin in muscles (Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2015b; Wu et al., 2012a).
evidence: Based on comparison with published phenotypes of muscle-specific β-catenin mutants

claim: Wnt7A can initiate both canonical and non-canonical pathways
source: Wnt7A has been reported to initiate both canonical and non-canonical pathway (Heasley and Winn, 2008; Posokhova et al., 2015; von Maltzahn et al., 2011; Winn et al., 2005; Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt7A signaling pathways

claim: Motoneuron-specific deletion of β-catenin does not impair NMJ development
source: However, motoneuron-specific deletion of β-catenin does not impair NMJ development (Li et al., 2008; Wu et al., 2015a), excluding a role of canonical pathway in motoneurons.
evidence: Based on cited literature on motoneuron-specific β-catenin knockout

claim: Wnt non-canonical JNK pathway regulates axonal transport of vesicles in C. elegans
source: Interestingly, Wnt non-canonical JNK pathway has been reported to regulate axonal transport of vesicles in C. elegans (Byrd et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt signaling in C. elegans

claim: Lack of Wnts from motoneurons may directly impair postsynaptic assembly
source: Because Wnts can directly regulate postsynaptic AChR assembly (Barik et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012), lack of Wnts from motoneurons may thus impair postsynaptic assembly.
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt regulation of AChR assembly and inference from the mutant phenotype

claim: Problems with presynaptic assembly may impair synaptic basal lamina
source: On the other hand, neurotransmission blockade by botulinum toxin disrupts NMJ morphology (Rogozhin et al., 2008). Problems with presynaptic assembly may impair synaptic basal lamina.
evidence: Based on cited literature and inference from observed basal lamina defects

claim: SV2 staining is progressively restricted from axon to nerve terminal during NMJ development
source: SV2 staining is progressively restricted from axon to the nerve terminal during NMJ development (Lupa and Hall, 1989). This is thought to indicate active vesicle transportation during neural development.
evidence: Based on cited literature on SV2 localization during development

claim: Increased vesicle proteins in axons may be indicative of axon regeneration in the absence of Wls
source: At the same, increased vesicle proteins in axons may be indicative of axon regeneration in the absence of Wls.
evidence: Based on observed increase in SV2 and Synapsin 1 in axons

claim: Axon terminal swellings and varicosities in HB9-Wls-/- mice resemble those of nerve degeneration during aging
source: Nevertheless, such axon terminals swellings and varicosities are observed in NMJs recovering from Botulinum toxin poisoning (Rogozhin et al., 2008) and resemble those of nerve degeneration during aging (Bhattacharya et al., 2016; Lüningschrör et al., 2017; Valdez et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on comparison with published phenotypes in other conditions

claim: The observations are indicative of reinnervation in response to functional denervation
source: Together, these observations are indicative of reinnervation in response to functional denervation.
evidence: Based on multiple observations including axonal swellings and increased vesicle proteins

claim: Individual Wnts have different sensitivities to Wls deficiency
source: Apparently, this might not be the case because individual Wnt has different sensitivities to Wls deficiency (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on Western blot analysis showing differential effects of Wls knockdown on different Wnts in Figure 7

claim: Zebrafish Wls mutants are surprisingly normal in early development, in contrast to Wnt5B and Wnt11 mutants
source: In agreement, Zebrafish Wls mutants are surprisingly normal in early development, in contrast to Wnt5B and Wnt11 mutants (Kuan et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited literature on zebrafish Wls mutants

claim: Some Wnts may be regulated in a Wls-independent manner
source: It is possible that some Wnts may be regulated in a Wls-independent manner.
evidence: Based on differential sensitivity of Wnts to Wls deficiency and literature on zebrafish

claim: Wls-antisense morpholino severely impairs membrane localization of Wnt5B but not Wnt11 in zebrafish
source: For example, Wls-antisense morpholino was shown to severely impair membrane localization of Wnt5B, but not Wnt11 in zebrafish (Wu et al., 2015a).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt localization in zebrafish

claim: WntD in Drosophila does not require lipidation by Porcupine and may be secreted independent of Wls
source: WntD in Drosophila does not require lipidation by Porcupine and thus may be secreted independent of Wls (Chen et al., 2012; Ching et al., 2008; Richards et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature on WntD secretion in Drosophila

claim: Wnt3A seems not responsive to Wls overexpression
source: Wnt3A seems not responsive to Wls overexpression (Galli et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt3A and Wls

claim: The NMJ is a synapse between motoneurons and skeletal muscles to control motor behavior
source: The neuromuscular junction (NMJ) is a synapse between motoneurons and skeletal muscles to control motor behavior.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about NMJ function

claim: Genetic evidence of Wnt in mammalian NMJ development was missing due to the existence of multiple Wnts and their receptors
source: Genetic evidence of Wnt in mammalian NMJ development was missing due to the existence of multiple Wnts and their receptors.
evidence: Based on the rationale for the study and known complexity of Wnt signaling

claim: Wls is a Wnt ligand secretion mediator
source: We show when Wnt secretion is abolished from motoneurons by mutating the Wnt ligand secretion mediator (Wls) gene, mutant mice showed muscle weakness and neurotransmission impairment.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about Wls function

claim: NMJs in HB9-Wls-/- mice were unstable with reduced synaptic junctional folds and fragmented AChR clusters
source: NMJs were unstable with reduced synaptic junctional folds and fragmented AChR clusters.
evidence: Based on morphological and EM analysis of NMJs in mutant mice

claim: Nerve terminals in HB9-Wls-/- mice were swollen with fewer and mislocated synaptic vesicles
source: Nerve terminals were swollen; synaptic vesicles were fewer and mislocated.
evidence: Based on morphological, EM, and immunostaining analysis

claim: Presynaptic deficits occurred earlier than postsynaptic deficits in HB9-Wls-/- mice
source: The presynaptic deficits occurred earlier than postsynaptic deficits.
evidence: Based on electrophysiological analysis at P1 and P30 showing temporal progression of deficits

claim: NMJ phenotypes were not observed when deleting Wls in muscles or Schwann cells
source: Intriguingly, these phenotypes were not observed when deleting Wls in muscles or Schwann cells.
evidence: Based on analysis of HSA-Wls-/- and Wnt1-Wls-/- mice

claim: Motoneuron Wnts are necessary for NMJ development, in particular presynaptic differentiation
source: These observations demonstrate a necessary role of motoneuron Wnts in NMJ development, in particular presynaptic differentiation.
evidence: Based on comprehensive findings showing predominantly presynaptic deficits in motoneuron-specific Wls knockout

claim: Dysfunction of the NMJ has been implicated in congenital myasthenia syndrome, myasthenia gravis, and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis
source: Dysfunction of this synapse has been implicated in various neurological disorders including congenital myasthenia syndrome (CMS), myasthenia gravis (MG), and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) (Li et al., 2018; Sanes and Lichtman, 2001; Shen et al., 2015; Wu et al., 2010).
evidence: Based on cited literature on NMJ-related disorders

claim: Motoneurons produce agrin that binds its receptor LRP4 in muscle fibers and activates MuSK
source: For example, motoneurons produce agrin that binds its receptor LRP4 (low-density lipoprotein receptor-related protein 4) in muscle fibers and activates the muscle specific kinase MuSK (Bezakova and Ruegg, 2003; DeChiara et al., 1996; Kim et al., 2008; McMahan, 1990; Zhang et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on cited literature on agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling

claim: The agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling is necessary for NMJ formation, in particular postsynaptic AChR clustering
source: The agrin-LRP4-MuSK signaling is necessary for NMJ formation, in particular postsynaptic AChR clustering.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about agrin-LRP4-MuSK pathway

claim: Much less is known about mechanisms of presynaptic assembly of the NMJ compared to postsynaptic differentiation
source: In contrast to postsynaptic differentiation, much less is known about mechanisms of presynaptic assembly of the NMJ.
evidence: Based on assessment of the state of knowledge in the field

claim: Wnts can induce AChR clusters by themselves in cultured C2C12 myotubes
source: Regarding NMJ development, Wnts can induce AChR clusters by themselves and can promote agrin-induced AChR clustering in cultured C2C12 myotubes (Barik et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt effects on AChR clustering

claim: Wnts can promote agrin-induced AChR clustering in cultured C2C12 myotubes
source: Regarding NMJ development, Wnts can induce AChR clusters by themselves and can promote agrin-induced AChR clustering in cultured C2C12 myotubes (Barik et al., 2014b; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt effects on AChR clustering

claim: The extracellular cysteine-rich domain of MuSK is homologous to that in the Wnt receptor Frizzled
source: These effects seem to require the extracellular cysteine-rich domain (CRD) of MuSK, which is homologous to that in the Wnt receptor Frizzled (Hubbard and Gnanasambandan, 2013).
evidence: Based on cited literature on MuSK structure

claim: Deleting the CRD of MuSK impairs in vivo NMJ formation
source: Deleting the CRD was shown to impair in vivo NMJ formation (Messéant et al., 2015; Strochlic et al., 2012) although this notion was challenged by another study (Remédio et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited literature with conflicting findings on MuSK CRD function

claim: MuSK interacts with disheveled (Dvl1), the key scaffold protein in the Wnt signal pathway
source: Intracellularly, MuSK interacts with disheveled (Dvl1), the key scaffold protein in the Wnt signal pathway (Luo et al., 2002).
evidence: Based on cited literature on MuSK-Dvl1 interaction

claim: In Zebrafish, Wnt binding to the CRD of MuSK and MuSK interaction with Dvl are necessary for guiding axons to the middle region of muscle fibers
source: In Zebrafish, Wnt binding to the CRD of MuSK and MuSK interaction with Dvl are necessary for guiding axons to the middle region of muscle fibers (Jing et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature on zebrafish NMJ development

claim: Mutant mice lacking or overexpressing β-catenin in muscle fibers display both pre- and postsynaptic deficits
source: Mutant mice lacking or overexpressing β-catenin, a key mediator of the Wnt canonical pathway, in muscle fibers display both pre- and postsynaptic deficits (Li et al., 2008; Liu et al., 2012; Wu et al., 2012a).
evidence: Based on cited literature on β-catenin mutant mice

claim: Dvl1 expresses higher in axons than dendrites, especially in growth cones of cultured hippocampus neurons
source: In terms of synapses in the brain, Dvl1 expresses higher in axons than dendrites, especially in growth cones of cultured hippocampus neurons, suggesting a role of Wnt pathway in presynaptic differentiation (Zhang et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Dvl1 localization in neurons

claim: Cerebella granule cells secret Wnt7A to induce axon and growth cone remodeling, including Synapsin 1 puncta clustering
source: Cerebella granule cells secret Wnt7A to induce axon and growth cone remodeling, including Synapsin 1 puncta clustering (Hall et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt7A effects in cerebellar neurons

claim: Inducing the expression of Dickkopf1 decreases the number of cortico-striatal synapses in adult mice
source: Inducing the expression of Dickkopf1, a secreted Wnt antagonist, decreases the number of cortico-striatal synapses in adult mice.
evidence: Based on cited literature on Dickkopf1 effects on synapses

claim: Excitatory terminals in Dickkopf1-expressing mice contain fewer synaptic vesicles
source: The remaining excitatory terminals contain fewer synaptic vesicles (Galli et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Dickkopf1 effects on synaptic vesicles

claim: There are 19 different Wnts in rodents and humans
source: There are 19 different Wnts in rodents and humans (Barik et al., 2014b), many of which have redundant functions, making it difficult to reveal convincingly the function of Wnt ligands in vivo.
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wnt family members

claim: Many Wnts have redundant functions, making it difficult to reveal the function of Wnt ligands in vivo
source: There are 19 different Wnts in rodents and humans (Barik et al., 2014b), many of which have redundant functions, making it difficult to reveal convincingly the function of Wnt ligands in vivo.
evidence: Based on cited literature and known challenges in studying Wnt function

claim: Wls is a seven-transmembrane protein necessary for sorting and transporting Wnts from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface
source: Wls is a seven-transmembrane protein that is necessary for sorting and transporting Wnts from the endoplasmic reticulum to the cell surface (Hausmann et al., 2007).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wls structure and function

claim: In Drosophila Wls mutants, Wingless is retained intracellularly and cannot be secreted
source: In Drosophila Wls mutants, Wingless (the homolog of vertebrate Wnt1) is retained intracellularly and cannot be secreted (Bänziger et al., 2006; Bartscherer et al., 2006; Goodman et al., 2006).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Drosophila Wls mutants

claim: Wls null mouse embryos exhibit defects in establishment of the body axis
source: Wls null mouse embryos exhibit defects in establishment of the body axis (Fu et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited literature on Wls null mice

claim: Dysregulation of Wnt signaling is a pathological mechanism of neuromuscular disorders
source: Our results support a model where motoneurons secret Wnts such as Wnt7A and Wnt7B for nerve terminal differentiation, suggesting dysregulation of Wnt signaling as a pathological mechanism of neuromuscular disorders.
evidence: Based on the findings of the study showing NMJ deficits when Wnt secretion is blocked
